content: Murrain, pronounced mur'in, is a highly contagious disease that affects cattle and sheep. The term murrain literally translates to disease and was commonly used during medieval times to describe any illness affecting livestock. During that era, people lacked the ability to distinguish between specific diseases in their animals, so they grouped all such illnesses under the general term murrain. Significant outbreaks of murrain occurred in Europe during the 14th century. These outbreaks, combined with the climatic effects of the Little Ice Age, contributed to widespread famine during the Great Famine of 1315–1317. This period of famine significantly weakened the European population, leaving it more vulnerable to the devastating impact of the Black Death, which began in 1348. Murrain is also mentioned in the Bible in reference to the fifth plague inflicted upon Egypt. In Exodus 9:3, it is written: Behold, the hand of the LORD is upon thy cattle which is in the field, upon the horses, upon the asses, upon the camels, upon the oxen, and upon the sheep: there shall be a very grievous murrain. In certain regions of Scotland, it was believed that a practice known as force-fire could cure murrain.
